id: #104 from The Poems of Gaius Valerius Catullus

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

with Dana Ward with Dana Ward I have so little want of activity even writing with its pain more terrible than life I don’t want but do because I’m kind of stupid finally not in the way, you, Sarah know I am nor, you reader, who think of me fishing. Line, spindle, lure, bait. Instruments for me are accessories, even the matchbook is only a tiara to my eyes, the fishing lure a long & white bracelet. Some of my so-called friends think of me as a derelict they always try to hold me to account. “Tell me what happened on the drunken night in question” On the witness stand I am a kitten terribly cute but I can’t say a thing about stupid, or fish, or last night. I like to lay at the base of a hill asleep while the shepherds work bringing things to heel with tepid will where I source my contempt in the index of swill. The entries there make no mention of hell which was sifted through the vale of tears, & fell to make Earth, & the base of this hill where I sunbathe & murmur ‘jealous cellmate’ as my willful peers go by.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Dana, Ward, Sarah

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text, refined for eloquence and flow while preserving its original imagery, tone, and meaning:

---

**with Dana Ward**

with Dana Ward

I have so little desire for activity—even writing, with its pain more terrible than life itself, is something I don't want yet do anyway, out of a kind of foolishness. This isn't lost on you, Sarah, who know me, nor on you, the reader, imagining me out fishing. Line, spindle, lure, bait—for me these instruments are mere accessories; even the matchbook appears to my eyes as nothing more than a tiara, the fishing lure a long, white bracelet.

Some of my so-called friends regard me as a derelict, forever trying to hold me accountable. *"Tell me what happened on the drunken night in question."* On the witness stand, I become a kitten—terribly cute, yet unable to utter a word about foolishness, or fish, or the night before.

I prefer to lie at the base of a hill, asleep, while the shepherds labor above, bringing all things to heel with their tepid will—there, in that index of swill, I find the source of my contempt. Its entries make no mention of hell, which was sifted through the vale of tears and fell to form the Earth, and the base of this very hill where I sunbathe, murmuring *"jealous cellmate"* as my willful peers pass by.
outputs.L2:
With Dana Ward, with Dana Ward

My appetite for doing anything is nearly nonexistent—even putting words on paper, agonizing as it is, worse than existence itself. I resist it, yet I comply anyway, driven by my own foolishness—not foolish in the sense you mean, Sarah, nor in the way you, the one reading this, picture me out fishing. Rod, reel, hook, worm—to me these tools are mere ornaments. Even a book of matches looks like a crown in my eyes; the fishing hook resembles nothing more than an elegant white bangle.

Certain acquaintances of mine regard me as worthless, constantly demanding explanations from me. "Describe exactly what took place that night you were drunk." Placed under questioning, I transform into something adorable and helpless—a small cat—utterly unable to speak about foolishness, or fishing, or the events of the previous evening.

I prefer to stretch out and doze near the foot of a hill while others—shepherds—labor away, herding their flocks with half-hearted commitment. This is where my bitterness originates, cataloged among life's refuse. Nowhere in that catalog does hell appear—hell, which was strained through countless tears before descending to form this Earth, and this very hillside where I bask in sunlight, whispering "envious fellow prisoner" as my headstrong companions pass me by.
outputs.L3:
# On the Reluctant Poet: An Exploration of Self, Labor, and Contempt

The speaker's relationship to writing emerges as one steeped in ambivalence, even antagonism. Writing is not framed as a calling or a gift but as an affliction—something painful, laborious, almost punishing. And yet the speaker persists, not out of inspiration or joy, but out of what they themselves diagnose as a kind of stupidity, a compulsion they cannot fully justify or escape. This self-deprecating framing sets the tone for the entire work: writing becomes an act performed despite oneself, a stubborn habit rather than a noble pursuit, and the speaker's awareness of this irony only deepens the sense of resigned self-mockery that pervades the piece.

This same impulse toward reinvention and displacement extends to the speaker's treatment of ordinary objects. Fishing instruments, matchbooks, and lures—items defined by their utility, their purpose within a practical world of labor and survival—are stripped of function and recast as ornaments. They become decorative, almost talismanic, valued not for what they do but for what they represent or how they appear. This transformation mirrors the speaker's broader tendency to resist conventional purpose, whether in objects or in life itself, favoring aesthetic or symbolic value over productive use.

This resistance to purpose and accountability carries into the speaker's social world as well. Friends perceive the speaker as something of a derelict, someone who fails to meet expectations of responsibility or explanation. There is pressure placed upon the speaker to account for their behavior—most pointedly, to explain away a "drunken night" that seems to hang over them as evidence of dissolution or failure. Yet the speaker refuses this reckoning, remaining evasive, slippery, almost willfully incomprehensible. The comparison to "a kitten" is telling: it suggests innocence, playfulness, and a kind of disarming irresponsibility, as though the speaker can dodge serious scrutiny by retreating into childlike behavior, avoiding the adult burden of justification.

This evasiveness is further dramatized through the poem's central image of contrast: the speaker lounging passively at the base of a hill, sunbathing, inert, while shepherds labor actively above, driving their flocks, imposing order, discipline, and structure onto the world—"bringing things to heel." The juxtaposition is stark. Where the shepherds embody purposeful labor and control, the speaker embodies stillness, idleness, a refusal to participate in the disciplined shaping of experience. This passive existence becomes both a source of freedom and an implicit critique, positioning the speaker as an outsider to the structured, productive world the shepherds represent.

Finally, the speaker situates their own bitterness and cynicism—the "swill" of contempt that colors their worldview—not within any traditional or mythic conception of hell, but within a personal, lived history of suffering that feels uniquely their own. This is not damnation in a religious sense but a private hell, constructed from personal experience and disillusionment. From this vantage point, the speaker looks upon more disciplined, willful peers—those who embody the same order and control seen in the shepherds—not with admiration but with dismissive scorn, labeling them "jealous cellmates." This phrase suggests a shared confinement, a mutual imprisonment within circumstance or expectation, yet one in which the speaker imagines their peers as envious of the very freedom or recklessness that the speaker's derelict, undisciplined existence affords. In this final gesture, the poem crystallizes its central tension: the uneasy pride the speaker takes in their own failure to conform, even as that failure isolates them within a private, self-authored hell.
outputs.L4:
# Expanding on Dana Ward's Poetic Exploration of Passivity and Resistance

Dana Ward's poem constructs an intricate meditation on the politics of refusal, using a distinctly fragmented and surreal narrative voice to interrogate the space between action and inaction. Rather than presenting a linear argument or confessional narrative, the poem moves associatively—drifting between images and moments that resist easy synthesis. This formal fragmentation is not merely stylistic; it enacts the very passivity and evasiveness the poem thematizes, allowing the reader to experience the speaker's resistance to coherence as a lived, textual reality rather than simply reading about it.

Central to the poem's imaginative logic is its transformation of ordinary, overlooked objects into charged symbols of withdrawal. Fishing gear—typically associated with patience, waiting, and a kind of purposeful stillness—becomes emblematic of a deeper existential loitering, a suspension of productive action that borders on the meditative. Matchbooks, small and disposable, evoke fleeting moments of ignition and extinguishing, suggesting the poem's interest in brief flares of potential meaning that never quite catch into full significance. These mundane objects, recontextualized through the poem's associative logic, come to represent an aesthetic of detachment: a way of being in the world that prioritizes drift and observation over decisive engagement or explanation.

This detachment finds its most striking articulation in the poem's central image: the speaker's comparison of themselves to a kitten unable to testify. This figure captures something essential about the poem's stance toward accountability and self-justification. A kitten, after all, cannot explain its behavior—it simply acts according to impulse, instinct, and whim, existing entirely outside the discourse of justification that structures human social life. By aligning the speaker with this pre-linguistic, pre-rational figure, Ward suggests a deliberate retreat from the expectation that one must always account for oneself, must always render one's choices legible and defensible to others.

This refusal to explain becomes, paradoxically, a form of agency. The poem suggests that embracing ambiguity and idleness—rather than succumbing to the pressure of constant self-justification—constitutes a quiet but meaningful rebellion. In a culture that often demands productivity, transparency, and accountability as markers of social legitimacy, the speaker's insistence on remaining opaque, unexplained, and unproductive becomes a subtle act of resistance. This is not the loud, declarative rebellion of protest or manifesto, but something more understated: a passive-aggressive withholding that asserts autonomy precisely through its refusal to participate in the expected rituals of explanation.

Ultimately, the poem stages a tension between societal expectations of coherence, productivity, and accountability, and an inner resistance that manifests as idleness, ambiguity, and self-doubt. This tension is never fully resolved; instead, it remains suspended, much like the poem's own fragmented structure. In this way, Ward's work becomes both a description and an enactment of resistance—demonstrating through its very form the kind of quiet, unexplained defiance that its content explores, and inviting readers to sit with the discomfort of unresolved meaning rather than seeking premature clarity or closure.
outputs.L5:
# A Chance Encounter

Dana had been working at the community center for nearly three years when Ward first walked through the doors. He was looking for volunteer opportunities, something to fill his weekends now that his children had grown and moved away. Dana, who coordinated the volunteer programs, immediately saw potential in his quiet enthusiasm.

"We could use someone with your background in carpentry," Dana said, reviewing his application. "We're building a new playground next month, and Sarah's been struggling to find enough hands."

Sarah, who ran the youth outreach program, arrived just as Dana mentioned her name. She overheard the conversation and smiled.

"Perfect timing," Sarah said, extending her hand to Ward. "We need someone who actually knows what they're doing. Last time, I nearly built a slide that led nowhere."

Ward laughed, immediately at ease with the two women who clearly worked well together, finishing each other's sentences and sharing an easy rapport built from years of collaboration.

Over the following weeks, the three of them became an unlikely but effective team. Dana handled the logistics and scheduling, making sure volunteers showed up when needed and materials arrived on time. Sarah focused on the children, gathering their ideas about what they wanted in their new play space—complete with hand-drawn sketches that grew increasingly ambitious. Ward brought it all to life, translating scribbled crayon dreams into structurally sound reality.

By the time the playground opened, something had changed. What started as a simple volunteer arrangement had grown into genuine friendship. Dana often remarked that she couldn't remember a project that had brought her as much joy. Sarah agreed, noting how the children's laughter as they tested the new equipment made every difficult moment worthwhile.

Ward, for his part, found something he hadn't realized he was missing—a sense of purpose and community that had felt distant since retirement. Dana and Sarah had welcomed him not just as a volunteer, but as a partner in building something meaningful.

The playground still stands today, a testament to what happens when the right people find each other at the right moment—Dana's organization, Sarah's compassion, and Ward's craftsmanship combining to create something none of them could have built alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, stream-of-consciousness poem dedicated "with Dana Ward" that blends confessional self-deprecation with dreamlike imagery of fishing tackle and jewelry.
counterfactuals.output:
**with Dana Ward**

I keep my worst thoughts in a tackle box lined with velvet
like it's a ring I'm too embarrassed to propose with,
hooks nestled next to garnets, a treble hook snagged
on the fine gold chain my grandmother wore into the ground—
I'm not saying I'm a fisherman, I'm saying I've been dangling
the same lure of myself over the same dark water for years
and something keeps almost biting, some tenderness
shaped like a trout, shaped like the last good feeling
I had in 2004, and I reel it in slow because I read somewhere
that's how you don't lose them, the fish or the feelings,
though I've lost both, repeatedly, the way you lose
an earring in a couch you didn't know had that kind
of hunger in it—

Dana, if you're in this poem it's because I wanted witnesses,
someone to see me tie a bad knot in the monofilament
of my personality and call it a lure, call it "attractive,"
a sinker dressed up like a locket, a swivel clasp
doing the emotional labor of an actual swivel—

I want to say I'm evolving but mostly I'm just
rearranging the tackle box, moving the spinnerbait
next to the cheap zirconia ring I bought myself
after a bad year, both of them glinting under the one bulb
in my kitchen like they're in on something I'm not,
like the fish and the finger both know
what it means to be caught, to be worn,
to be the thing somebody almost wanted enough to keep.

Somewhere a hook opens like a question mark
into water that doesn't answer, and I dangle there too,
barbed and gleaming, hoping someone mistakes me
for treasure long enough to reel me toward the light,
gut me gently, find nothing inside but more small hooks,
more cheap rings, more of this glittering, useless tackle
I call a self and keep casting anyway, again,
again, into you, into the pond, into the poem,
hoping something with a mouth
finds me irresistible today.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental poem in the style of contemporary poet Dana Ward, mixing casual conversational asides with dense lyrical metaphor, addressing an unnamed "Sarah."
counterfactuals.output:
**Notes for Sarah, Written While the Coffee Goes Cold**

Sarah, I keep starting this poem the way you start
a car you're not sure will turn over—hopeful,
half-apologetic, one hand already
on the door in case I need to get out and push.

It's Tuesday, or the emotional equivalent of Tuesday,
which is any day that arrives without ceremony
and asks you to be a person in it anyway.

I want to tell you about the light this morning,
how it came through the blinds in strips
like it was trying to bar itself from the room,
like even the sun has days it doesn't want
full participation, just wants to lean
against the doorframe of the sky
and watch everyone else be alive for a while—

but that's a lie, sort of, because the light
was just light, ordinary, indifferent,
and I'm the one who needed it to mean something
because you didn't text back and I was busy
turning silence into astronomy.

Sarah, do you ever feel like a comma
in someone else's sentence—necessary,
barely visible, load-bearing in a way
no one will thank you for?

I had a dream you were a lighthouse
but not metaphorically, just literally,
you were standing in the harbor
made entirely of glass and warning,
and boats keep their distance from you
not because you're dangerous
but because you're the only fixed thing
for miles and everyone's afraid
of what fixed things ask of them—
permanence, or at least
the pretense of it.

(I should say—this isn't about you, exactly.
It's about the shape your absence makes,
which is its own weather system,
its own low-pressure front
moving quietly through my Tuesday.)

I keep thinking about how the body
is just a coastline for whatever's inside trying
to leave, how grief moves like tide,
recedes enough you think it's gone
and then it's back, dragging
the whole ocean's argument behind it.

Sarah, if this poem were honest
it would just be your name
repeated forty times
in decreasing font size
until it disappeared into the white
the way certain frequencies disappear
into other frequencies, not gone,
just no longer legible to whatever's listening.

Anyway. The coffee's cold.
I should probably finish it anyway—
some things you drink
not because they're good
but because you already poured them,
because the pouring was its own commitment,
because to waste it now
would mean admitting
the wanting was never
really about the coffee.

Sarah, wherever you are,
I hope the light finds you
strip by strip, ordinary,
indifferent, entirely
enough.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a free-verse piece that opens with a dedication to another poet, includes a mock courtroom interrogation scene, and ends with imagery of lying on a hill among shepherds.
counterfactuals.output:
**Deposition, with Sheep**
*for Ilya Kaminsky, who taught me that silence also testifies*

I.

They called me to the stand before I had
a name for what I'd seen. The gavel
was a heartbeat somebody else was having.

*State your relationship to the wound,*
said the judge, whose face was my father's face
wearing a wig made of unanswered letters.

*I was standing near it,* I said. *I was standing
near it and it got into my mouth.*

II.

*Let the record show the witness is evasive.
Let the record show the witness keeps saying "light"
when asked to describe the door.*

I said: the door was closed the way a hand
closes around something it's ashamed to drop.

*Strike that.*

*Tell the court where you were on the night
in question, the night of the actual world.*

I was here. I have always only been here,
holding my one lantern of syntax,
walking it back and forth across the evidence.

III.

*Approach the bench.*

I approached the bench. It was a fence.
It was a low stone wall somewhere outside the city
where no one had thought to build a courtroom yet.

The judge took off the wig. Underneath,
more wig. Underneath that, wind.

*This court finds insufficient grounds
to hold you further from the hillside.*

IV.

So I walked out past the folding chairs,
past the bailiff counting his rosary of keys,
out through a door that turned out to be weather,

and there were the shepherds, unbothered,
their fires small and orange as a held breath,
their sheep like paragraphs the dark had softened.

No one asked me to testify to the grass.
No one asked me to prove the stars.

I lay down among them on the hill,
my ribs still ringing faintly like a bell
someone rang in another century by mistake,

and one shepherd passed me bread
without asking what I'd done to deserve it,
and one dog put its head against my hand
as if my hand were a sentence it could trust,

and above us the whole story kept revising itself,
quietly, in light,
the way snow rewrites a field
without once being asked
to explain itself in court.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem exploring themes of laziness, self-contempt, and evasion of accountability, using odd juxtapositions like calling a matchbook a "tiara" and comparing oneself to a kitten on a witness stand.
counterfactuals.output:
**Deposition of a Houseplant**

I wear the matchbook like a tiara,
crowned in things I meant to burn—
the emails, the apologies, the gym membership
that autorenewed my guilt every month like clockwork
I never wound.

Call me to the stand.
I'll take the oath like a kitten takes a bath:
badly, with visible betrayal,
one paw already planning
its escape through the window
of "I didn't know that was due today."

Your Honor, I'd like to enter into evidence
this couch cushion, exhibit A,
shaped now like the absence of a person
who lived here in theory.
I plead the fifth. I plead the fetal position.
I plead general vagueness,
the specific innocence of moss—
growing, sure, but so slowly
it's basically not growing at all.

I am not lazy. I am *conserving*.
Like a bear. Like a bear who filed for extension
on hibernation, on every winter,
on the entire concept of waking up
prepared.

The tiara slips. It was always
just cardboard and half-used promises.
I strike a match against my own name
and let it flare, brief and useless,
proof I *could* have done something
with my hands
besides holding them up, empty,
to a jury of one—
myself, unimpressed,
banging the gavel of *whatever, later*
until the courtroom empties
and only the kitten remains,
licking its paw,
already forgetting
what it was accused of.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract, associative poem in a New York School–influenced voice, incorporating direct address, biblical undertones (vale of tears, hell, Earth), and a closing image of watching "willful peers" pass by.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ash Wednesday on Sixth Avenue**

Listen—I wasn't born to explain the vale of tears
to you, though here we are, ankle-deep
in it, the coffee cart guy's radio
preaching something about fire and how
it doesn't consume the bush, just lights it
like a cigarette held too long between two fingers.

You always did have a talent for standing
in doorways as if they were thresholds
of something larger, Ohio maybe, or heaven,
which I hear is just Ohio with better light.

I keep thinking hell is a waiting room
with a number system nobody explains,
and Earth is the little joke god tells
before the real punchline, the one
where we all get up and go to work anyway,
carrying our small fires in paper cups.

Somewhere it is written that we are dust,
but here, now, we are mostly wool coats
and the smell of someone else's lunch,
and I love you the way you love
a intersection—instinctively, without asking why
the light changes.

If this is a vale, then let's call the buildings
its walls, let's call the pigeons its angels,
unimpressive and everywhere, muttering.

I have no theology except this:
that I sat on the steps and did not move
while the whole avenue
kept walking—

and I watched them go, my willful peers,
their coats a little brighter than the cold,
their faces already somewhere else,
already forgiven for something
they didn't know they'd done.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
